title: Merge Intervals
statement: You get a list of intervals, each a pair [start, end], in no particular order. Join every group of intervals that overlap into one interval, and return the joined list. Two intervals that only touch at one point, like [1, 2] and [2, 3], count as overlapping.

example.caption: [1,3] and [2,4] overlap, so they become [1,4]. [5,6] stands alone.

idea.sentence: Sort by start, then each interval either overlaps the last merged one (its start is at or before that end) or begins a fresh one.

jargon.plain: Two sorted intervals overlap when the later start is at or before the earlier end. Here, equal counts too.
One interval that covers a whole chain of overlapping ones: smallest start, largest end.

watch.inputHint: One argument: a list of [start, end] pairs, e.g. [[1,3],[5,6],[2,4]]

compare.bruteLabel: Compare every pair, repeat until stable

rows.name: Compare all pairs
rows.note: Merge any two that overlap and keep going until nothing changes.

rows.name: Sort, then sweep
rows.note: The sort dominates. The sweep is one pass and only looks at the last merged interval.

fast.takeaway: Sorting turns a many-to-many question into a neighbour question: only the last merged interval can overlap the next one.

stages.title: Sort by start
stages.note: Sort a copy, with a numeric comparator, so overlapping intervals end up side by side.

stages.title: Overlap test
stages.note: Is the next start at or before the end of the last merged interval? Touching counts.

stages.title: Stretch
stages.note: Overlap: set the last end to the larger of the two ends. A contained interval must not shrink it.

stages.title: Start a new one
stages.note: Gap: push a fresh copy of the interval as a new merged interval.

stages.title: Return
stages.note: Every interval has been folded in. The result list is the answer.

edges.title: Touching ends
edges.why: The test is start <= end, not start < end. Sharing the point 2 is enough to join them.

edges.title: One swallows another
edges.why: The second end (3) is smaller than 10. Use max, never just assign the new end.

edges.title: Unsorted input
edges.why: Without sorting, [10,12] would be checked before [9,11]. Sort first, and sort by number.

edges.title: Empty list
edges.why: There is no first interval to read. The loop never runs and the empty result is returned.

gotchas.text: arr.sort() with no comparator sorts as strings, so 10 comes before 9. Always pass (a, b) => a[0] - b[0].

sort() changes the array in place, which would reorder the caller's list. Copy first with [...intervals]. Also push [start, end] as a new array: pushing the input's own pair and then stretching it edits the input.
sort.Slice reorders the slice you pass in, and the caller shares that memory. Copy the outer slice first with append([][]int(nil), intervals...).
append(res, cur) stores the input's own inner slice, so later res[i][1] = ... also edits the input. Append a new []int{start, end}. Start res as [][]int{} so an empty answer is [] and not null.
Decide the touching rule first. Here [1,2] and [2,3] merge (<=). The same test with < would leave them apart.

recap.key: After sorting by start, the next interval either overlaps the last merged one (start <= its end) or starts a new one.
recap.complexity: Time O(n log n). Space O(n).
moves: Sort a copy by start (numeric comparator)
If next start <= last end, set last end = max(last end, end)
